references.text: The Preacher uses the wind as a metaphor for what is incomprehensible to humans: 'The wind blows toward the south and turns toward the north, it whirls around and around while blowing, and returns again on its paths.' The motif of the wind parallels Jesus' image of the wind that blows where it wishes, without anyone knowing where it comes from or where it goes (Ecclesiastes 1:6).

The Preacher compares the unknown to the wind and a fetus in the womb: 'Just as you do not know how the wind moves or how bones form in the womb of a pregnant woman, so too you cannot understand God's work, who does all things.' This expresses the same mystery that Jesus points to—that the Spirit's activity is unfathomable (Ecclesiastes 11:5).

In Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, God commands the prophet to speak to the spirit/wind (ruach) so that it blows over the dead and gives them life. The Hebrew word 'ruach' means both wind and spirit, just as the Greek 'pneuma' in John 3:8, highlighting the Spirit's life-giving and sovereign power (Ezekiel 37:9-10).
God promises to put His Spirit within His people so that they may live. This points to the new birth of the Spirit that Jesus speaks about in His conversation with Nicodemus (Ezekiel 37:14).

Jesus' words that one must be born of water and the Spirit to enter God's kingdom provide the immediate context for the wind metaphor in verse 8. The Spirit's sovereign work in regeneration is further explained through this wind imagery (John 3:5-6).

John's prologue states that believers are 'born of God'—not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man. This underscores the same divine sovereignty in regeneration that the wind image in John 3:8 illustrates (John 1:13).

Paul writes that only God's Spirit knows what belongs to God, which aligns with Jesus' words that no one knows where the wind comes from or where it goes—the Spirit's work is hidden from human understanding (1 Corinthians 2:11).

The Spirit distributes spiritual gifts to each person 'as He wills.' This reflects the sovereignty of the Spirit that Jesus describes using the wind image—the Spirit acts freely according to His own will (1 Corinthians 12:11).

At Pentecost, there came 'a sound from heaven like a mighty rushing wind,' and the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit. The physical wind as a sign of the Spirit's coming mirrors the wind image Jesus used in His conversation with Nicodemus (Acts 2:2-4).

James writes that God 'willed it so, and He gave us birth through the word of truth.' This points to God's sovereign will in regeneration, which corresponds with the point of the wind image that the Spirit works where He wills (James 1:18).

'Everyone born of God does not sin.' The expression 'born of God' (γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ) uses the same construction as 'born of the Spirit' (γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος) in John 3:8 and further explains what it means to be born again (1 John 3:9).
